s0.why: 1 defines a fault as a planar fracture in a volume of rock with significant displacement across it; flat is a fair paraphrase of planar.

s1.why: 11 has friction stopping movement and 13 has stress building on a locked fault until it ruptures and releases energy as seismic waves, forming an earthquake.

s2.why: 27 gives hanging wall up for reverse and down for normal; 30 gives lateral motion with little vertical movement for strike-slip.

f0.why: 12 calls the locked regions of higher friction asperities.

f1.why: 18 defines throw as the vertical displacement and heave as the horizontal component.

f2.why: 25 says the hanging wall and footwall terminology comes from mining.

f3.why: 4 says faults may also displace slowly by aseismic creep.

f4.why: 2 says the largest faults form the boundaries between the plates.

q1.why: 24 puts the hanging wall above the fault plane and 27 and 40 say it moves downward in a normal fault.

q2.why: 11 says friction can stop all movement and 13 says stress builds on the locked fault until it ruptures.

q3.why: 30 describes a near-vertical strike-slip fault moving laterally with very little vertical motion; the fence is setting.

q4.why: 42 defines a graben as a downthrown block between two normal faults dipping toward each other; 43 gives the horst contrast.

q5.why: 25 says the terms come from mining, with the footwall under the miner's feet and the hanging wall above; 'tilted' loosely renders 'tabular' but the answer stands.

q6.why: 38 says a reversal between tensional and compressional stress can reactivate faults with inverted movement; 39 says a normal fault may become reverse.
